summary: Proposes NETED, a common context editor with the same user interface on all servers, following surprising agreement on the idea at a resource sharing workshop. It was part of a broader proposal for a unified user-level protocol. The RFC is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 569 proposes NETED, a simple editor that could behave the same on different network servers. It is now Historic, and the author intended it as an easy-to-implement option rather than the only network editor.

questions: what were the neted editing modes
subtitle: A proposal for one simple text editor interface across network servers.

tldr.problem: People using several network servers had to learn each server's editor commands, and the author saw this as a barrier for users who were not professional programmers.
tldr.mechanism: Padlipsky proposes NETED, a simple line-oriented context editor based on the Multics eds editor, with input and edit modes and a defined set of requests.
tldr.outcome: RFC 569 is Historic. Its author presents NETED as a simple common model, not as the one definitive network editor.

today: RFC 569 is Historic. The unit lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: A Common Editor for Network Users
sections.content:
Padlipsky reports agreement at a resource-sharing workshop and in the Network User Interest Group that a common editor interface would be useful. Users who worked with several servers otherwise faced different editor conventions on each system.

He emphasizes the needs of people who are not professional programmers and may want to create or edit files without learning many unrelated interfaces. A common editor was also intended to make ordinary tasks such as preparing mail or program source possible across systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Each server could have different editing commands, which made it harder to move between systems. NETED proposes one familiar set of commands for basic file editing.

sections.title: The NETED Editor
sections.content:
NETED is based on Multics's eds, a line-oriented context editor. It has an input mode for entering text and an edit mode for changing a working copy of a file. In edit mode, a current-line pointer determines where many requests act.

The requests move through lines, locate text, move to the top or bottom, enter input mode, insert or replace a line, print lines, change text, delete lines, write the working copy, and save and exit. The proposal favors using the documented editor model rather than extending it with debated features.
sections.plainLanguage: NETED lets users enter text and then edit it by moving to lines, finding text, inserting, replacing or deleting. A user can write the working copy or save it and leave the editor.

sections.title: A Deliberately Limited Design
sections.content:
The author does not present NETED as “the” network editor. Its limited feature set is deliberate: he wants an editor that is simple for users and straightforward for implementors. He argues that adding features can lead to extended disputes about commands and behavior.

The Multics program listing is offered as a model for implementors, while the functional description could also guide a separate implementation. The RFC invites system programmers to respond with support, questions or reasoned objections.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal keeps NETED small so sites could implement it without lengthy design debates. The author invites other sites to evaluate the idea and respond.

sections.title: Creating and Editing Files
sections.content:
When NETED is started with the name of a file that does not exist, it enters input mode; the user types text into a working copy and leaves input mode with a line containing a period. Starting with an existing file enters edit mode, where the user issues requests on separate lines.

The current-line pointer can move forward or backward, and a locate request searches from its current position. The w request writes the working copy but leaves NETED running; save writes it and exits. The RFC warns that quitting through the TELNET Interrupt Process command loses the work in the working copy while leaving the original file intact.
sections.plainLanguage: A new file starts in text-entry mode; an existing file starts ready for editing. Users can save their changes or write a copy while staying in the editor.

references.text: Multics Programmer's Manual, Chapter 4, Part I, pages 24–54.
